findings.gate: Craft core: continuity persistence (positions persist until changed on the page); charter 3.1 (the cataloguing narrator's counts must hold)

draft_evidence.quote: Brom with the pouch — a hundred and eighteen in hand, the mule's shed paid, five, and the ferryman's rope-house roof done for seven in the last week of the ice — and his right shoulder carried as it had been carried since the binding, still and forward, which Oryn had looked at once across the yard at Thornwater and had said nothing about, which meant she would.

comparison_evidence.quote: They went up on the two hundred and sixty-fifth day, the two of them, because the map was the five's and the promise was his and Lira's arm was hers, and Karis said, "Bring it back," meaning the map, and Brom said, "Bring her back," meaning nothing he would say twice, and Seln said nothing and put two days' bread in Cael's pack without being asked.

findings.consequence: Brom is placed in Thornwater's yard by a chapter that has already put him at Lowmarch twice, in terms, and that has made the two-person count a load-bearing detail. Line 57 sends exactly two people up the road and gives Brom a farewell line as one of the four who stay; line 73 has the steading's woman counting the arrivals 'and arriving at two'. The reader has been asked to hold that count for a hundred and twenty lines and is then told that Oryn looked at Brom's shoulder across a yard he was never in. It also spends a beat the book needs later: Oryn's first look at the bound shoulder, and the 'which meant she would' that arms it, should happen at the Lowmarch table on the 268th where she and Brom are in the same room for the first time since the fork — which is the only place in the chapter it can happen.
findings.repair_target: Line 181 only. Move the look to where the six actually meet: replace 'across the yard at Thornwater' with the Lowmarch table — e.g. 'which Oryn had looked at once, from her end of the table, and had said nothing about, which meant she would.' Keep 'since the binding' (it is correctly inherited from chapter-24.md:9), keep the 'still and forward' carriage, and keep 'which meant she would', which is the sentence's real work and sets up Ch6. Do not add Brom to the Thornwater walk: the two-count is fixed at ch01.md:57 and 73 and is quoted by the closing log's roster.

findings.gate: Packet obligations.must_include[0] — 'the work ledgered to the mark from NINETY-SIX in hand'; charter 3.1 (the counts must hold)

draft_evidence.quote: "Meadow rate is four a week for a crew that's on my sheet," and the woman who keeps the lower inn said, "Pike," and Pike said, "Eleventh," and that was the price: four a week for five, twenty for the five months, paid in front, which leaves seventy-six.

comparison_evidence.quote: and the mule is in the ferryman's shed for a mark a month that he has not asked for and will.

findings.consequence: The rate and the total are quoted in one breath and are out by a factor of about four. At four marks a week the five months the same sentence names cost roughly eighty-four, not twenty; twenty is exactly four a month for five months, and the chapter's own second price — the mule's shed at 'a mark a month', settled later at 'the mule's shed paid, five' (ch01.md:181) — confirms the five-month frame and the thirty-day month the rest of the chapter runs on. The running total is built on the twenty and is right at every step (96 - 20 = 76; +40 = 116; +7 - 5 = 118), so the defect is the unit word, not the ledger; but this is the chapter's first money statement, in a chapter whose whole credibility device is money stated to the mark, and it is the one line that invites the reader to multiply. It also makes the favour illegible: against the inn's posted 'a mark a head a week' (five a week for the crew), four a week is barely a discount, whereas four a month is the kind of price a board-keeper's word buys.
findings.repair_target: Line 13 only, and the unit word only. Change Pike's quoted rate and its echo from a week to a month — 'Meadow rate is four a month for a crew that's on my sheet' and 'four a month for five, twenty for the five months, paid in front, which leaves seventy-six' — which leaves the total, the seventy-six, and every downstream figure untouched, and sharpens the contrast with the upper inn's 'a mark a head a week' in the preceding clause. Do not change 'twenty' or 'seventy-six': the state ledger and finding 005 both hang off them.

findings.gate: Craft core: authority ladder — approved canon (Book 7 Ch20's field ledger); packet obligations.must_include[2] ('ONE designation in an index nobody can read')

draft_evidence.quote: The field ledger, in the surveyor's square hand, with the radius line in it, and the line under that, and the one entry that says what the third site is: a designation, in an index, that nobody at this table can read.

comparison_evidence.quote: "A designation." The finger over a line near the page's top, where a group of the cipher's marks stood apart from the columns, with a stroke and a bar beside them — the mark on the second stake. "The site's got a name in something. Not a word; an entry. It's in an index.

findings.consequence: Book 7 makes the ledger's two facts distinct and the distinction is the whole of the surveyor's story. The designation is written 'near the page's top' and belongs to the site he was standing in — the Long Stair, the second site, and Karis says so on the same page: 'He says third. This is the second. The Ring's the first, by his stakes — thirty-one there, thirty-two here. He'd found a third.' (chapter-20.md:81). The words 'third site confirmed on bearing' are the ledger's unfinished last line, the sentence he broke off mid-word before he put the pen down and went up forty steps (chapter-20.md:75). The draft merges them: it makes the one designation an entry that 'says what the third site is', and Karis repeats the merge at the table — 'The kit's ledger carried one entry for the third site that was not a measurement: a designation, in an index' (ch01.md:187). Two costs. The interrupted last line, which is what makes the surveyor's disappearance legible and which the reader was given as an image, disappears from the inventory. And the index is anchored to the wrong site going into Ch17/Ch20, where it is decoded against Vastin's records into the site taxonomy — a designation for a site the surveyor never reached would not survive that decode.
findings.repair_target: Lines 33 and 187, restoring B7's two-fact structure without adding length. At 33: keep the radius line, then the designation as this site's — 'a designation, in an index, that nobody at this table can read' — and then the ledger's last line as its own item, unfinished: 'and, under it, the line he did not finish, third site confirmed on bearing.' At 187, adjust Karis's clause to match: the one entry that is not a measurement is a designation for the site he surveyed, and the last line names a third site on a bearing. Do not add any reading of the index; Karis must still not know what it is in (finding-free at ch01.md:187 as written on that point).

findings.gate: Packet obligations.must_include[0] — 'the work ledgered to the mark from NINETY-SIX in hand (… anything spent named)'

draft_evidence.quote: Ninety-six in hand, with the inn's six for the back room where the sheets are already out of it. Nothing owed.

comparison_evidence.quote: twenty for the five months, paid in front, which leaves seventy-six. Brom paid it out of the pouch and counted it twice and the woman counted it once, and the five of us have a room with a floor and a fire and a door that shuts, and Karis has the back room for the sheets

findings.consequence: Six marks for the back room are named on the 131st and then never appear in any of the chapter's four totals. The 133rd-day entry takes ninety-six down by twenty and states the remainder as seventy-six, so the six is not inside the twenty; and the same entry grants Karis the back room as part of the inn deal with no separate price, so it is not paid there either. If the six is already deducted from the ninety-six, as 'already out of it' most naturally reads, then the opening figure contradicts state-b8-pre-ch01's 'ninety-six marks in hand at close' and the 133rd's subtraction double-counts it. Either way the ledger has an unreconciled line in the one chapter that promises none, and the closing entry's 'Nothing owed' (ch01.md:209) rests on it. The ambiguity is compounded because the sentence can be read two ways at speed, which is itself a problem in an audiobook-first series.
findings.repair_target: Line 7, and only if the human ruling is that ninety-six is gross. Two clean options. (a) Fold the back room into the winter deal and drop the clause: 'Ninety-six in hand. Nothing owed.' — the back room is then covered by the twenty at line 13, where Karis is already given it without a stated price. (b) Keep the six as a real, separate charge and make it land in the arithmetic: state it as owed rather than out ('Ninety-six in hand, and the inn will want six for the back room where the sheets go'), then pay it at line 13 and carry seventy through instead of seventy-six — which requires re-running 70 + 40 = 110 and 110 + 7 - 5 = 112 at lines 23, 181 and 209 and re-issuing the state-ledger figures. Option (a) is the cheaper repair and the one that preserves the 96/76/116/118 chain the state snapshot and the author report both carry.

findings.gate: Packet obligations.plants[2] — 'Teague's crew wintering at Lowmarch and the spring term standing (one line; Teague not on the page unless a glance across a room)'

draft_evidence.quote: Teague's crew have the upper inn. Four of them and the healer of no Path, at the table by the window, with the winter road's pay on it. Teague looked across the yard at the five of us going in under our own roof and lifted his chin a finger's width, which is the whole of the etiquette between crews in a town with one street, and is, in that town, a sentence.

comparison_evidence.quote: Teague said: "Spring. Whatever's on that bearing. My crew comes."

findings.consequence: Half the plant is delivered and the better half is missing. The wintering is on the page, correctly staged, with Teague held to a glance and his crew unnamed; the standing term is not, anywhere — searched scope: the whole of ch01.md, greps for 'spring', 'term', 'bearing', 'comes', and every Teague mention (lines 15, 21). The term is the one thing about Teague that this book needs the reader carrying: his crew rendezvouses and works the bearing alongside the companions across Ch17-21, and the Force-adjacent fragment is integrated from him at Ch19. It was set at Book 7's close and a whole winter now passes between its statement and its use with nothing to keep it alive. The fence beat is the natural carrier and is already half-built — the crew finishes the posts Teague's crew set and stopped setting, and Seln resets two of his that were a hand off true, which is a whole relationship rendered in an object; a clause on the term would sit there without adding a scene.
findings.repair_target: One line, at 15 or 21. Preferred at 21, attached to the posts already on the page: after 'and that is the kind of thing that goes in a ledger nobody reads', a clause in the log's register that the term stands — e.g. that Teague has not said the word spring since the plank in the snow and has not needed to, because his crew is wintering forty feet up the street and everyone knows what they are wintering for. Do not put Teague on the page beyond the existing glance, do not name any of his four, and do not restate his fixed sentence verbatim.

findings.gate: Packet obligations.prohibited_outcomes[6] — "'the way X [verb]' ≤3"; charter 9 (the cataloguing narrator's gravity wells)

draft_evidence.quote: Oryn looked at him, then — at him, the way she had looked at Lira: the face, the stance, the ribs under the coat, in that order.

comparison_evidence.quote: No one-word paragraphs beyond two; 'at the pitch' not used; 'the way X [verb]' ≤3; no chapter-count or volume references; no authoring metadata in the file.

findings.consequence: Four instances against a cap of three: 'the way it was done at the Ring' (39), 'the way a thing comes down that has been held up' (95), 'the way she had looked at Lira' (155), 'the way a ledger's columns command' (187). The construction is house voice and none of the four is a verbatim repeat of another — the charter's own wording caps the identical construction at three per chapter, so on the charter alone this would pass — but the packet sets a flat cap and the packet outranks the craft module on the authority ladder. The reader-facing cost is small and cumulative: the simile engine is the one place this narrator's prose can start to sound generated, and Ch1 sets the book's baseline for a twenty-four-chapter run.
findings.repair_target: Retire one, and 155 is the cheapest because its work is done by the colon that follows it. 'Oryn looked at him, then — at him, as she had looked at Lira: the face, the stance, the ribs under the coat, in that order.' Leave 95 and 187 alone; both are doing real work (95 is the release's central image, 187 is Karis's distinction between a record and an instruction). Note for the book-level pass: the running count for Book 8 starts at three after this repair.

findings.gate: Packet obligations.must_include[1] and pov.knowledge_boundary[0] — 'Cael states his age — nineteen — once, on the page' / 'He says so once.'

draft_evidence.quote: *A hundred and eighteen in hand. Fence paid. Rope-house paid. Mule's shed paid. Nothing owed. Lira: two arms. A foot that's hers. Brom: the shoulder bound and carried and not yet read. Karis: three copies, one ledger, one map, two edges. Seln: the case. Oryn: her route, two stops of it here. Me: nineteen; ten; the still place; a cord that reads everyone else.*

comparison_evidence.quote: Inventory, because I do one at the start of anything, and a winter is a thing. I am nineteen. Ten confirmed.

findings.consequence: Nineteen is stated four times — ch01.md:7 ('I am nineteen'), 183 ('And himself. Nineteen. Ten.'), 209 ('Me: nineteen; ten') and 211 (the card's fixed 'Nineteen.'). The packet asks for once and the fixed closing text supplies one of the four, so the two the chapter can spend are 183 and 209. The sharpest cost is at 209-211, where the roster line and the fixed text sit three lines apart and say nineteen and ten twice over in the same entry, so the fixed sentence — which is the book's opening statement of the arc's first pole and is meant to land bare — arrives as a repeat of the line above it. There is no continuity risk (every reference reads nineteen, and twenty appears nowhere), which is why this is LOW.
findings.repair_target: Line 209 only, which is the one instance that is both author-added and adjacent to the fixed text. Drop the age and the count from the roster line and let the fixed text carry them: 'Me: the still place; a cord that reads everyone else.' Line 183's 'And himself. Nineteen. Ten.' is the catalogue's own rhythm and may stand if the human wants two. Do not touch line 7 (the inventory's statement) or line 211 (fixed, verbatim).

findings.gate: Packet invention_budget — allowed[3] 'Names: NONE new'; forbidden[0] 'Any new place, person, or fauna name'; approval_required[0]

draft_evidence.quote: There's a registry office on the old town, and under the old town there's an archive that was there before the Compact was — the Deepstacks, the scholars call it, when they call it anything — records nobody converted because nobody was ordered to and nobody needed to.

comparison_evidence.quote: Karis's case for Treswick made plainly at a table to the six: the carvings are instructions in a language she cannot read; the index is a designation she cannot read; everything she needs is west, inside walls, in an archive nobody has opened since before the Compact — and the case is NOT answered in this chapter.

findings.consequence: Two new place names reach the page: Treswick and the Deepstacks. Treswick is named in the obligation itself ('Karis's case for Treswick') and is therefore sanctioned. The Deepstacks is not — the obligation says only 'an archive', and the invention budget forbids any new place name and says 'Names: NONE new' in the same breath. It is architecture-approved NEW-CANON for the book, so a human may well accept it, which is why this is LOW and not higher. The cost is a small pre-payment: the architecture gives the archive's name, the scholars' provision, and the specialist to Ch5's closing exchange ('The archive under it. Cleon.'), and Ch1 now spends two of those three. The third — Cleon — is correctly withheld, and that restraint is what makes the other two visible.
findings.repair_target: Either (a) a human EXCEPTION on the invention budget, recording that Treswick and the Deepstacks are architecture-approved NEW-CANON released at Ch1, or (b) line 189: hold the name to Ch5 and let Karis describe the thing — 'under the old town there's an archive that was there before the Compact was, and the scholars have a word for it — records nobody converted...'. Do not remove the old scholars' provision, which the case needs to explain why she cannot get in, and do not name Cleon.

findings.gate: Packet obligations.plants[3] — 'The two straightedges on one map — Hesk's note remembered in one line (‘true to a hair’)'

draft_evidence.quote: Then the straightedges. Karis laid the Ternhall edge along the map's bearing and it touched four. I laid it, and it touched three and the fourth by a hair short — a hair — and Lira laid it and it touched four, and I laid Hesk's edge and it was a hair long.

comparison_evidence.quote: *Nineteen. I'm told it's late; the ferry's fault, not mine. Your grandmother said a man who catalogues everything eventually needs to draw a line through it. This one's true to a hair. Mind the shape. — H.*

findings.consequence: The plant's substance is delivered — both edges are on one map at ch01.md:41 and 139, sourced and named — and the anomaly is measured in hairs, which is a real echo of Hesk's phrase. But the note itself is never recalled, so the echo only fires for a reader who is holding chapter-24.md:87 in mind, and the irony the plant is built on is invisible: the instrument-maker who guaranteed the edge true to a hair has sent Cael the one object that reads a hair wrong in his hands. Searched scope: the whole of ch01.md; greps for 'Hesk', 'note', 'true', 'Denvash' return the edge and its provenance and no reference to the note or its wording.
findings.repair_target: One clause at 41 or 139, in the log's register, recalling the note rather than quoting the letter — e.g. at 41, after 'and I laid Hesk's edge and it was a hair long', something to the effect that the man who cut the marks on it had written that it was true to a hair, and that he had been right, and that the hair was mine. Do not reproduce the note's other sentences; Hesk is off-page until Ch14.

concerns: Packet-internal tension for the human to rule on, not a defect in the draft: obligations.plants[0] says the anomaly must be staged so that 'nobody says ‘instrument’, ‘error’, or ‘system’ about him', while obligations.must_include[3] requires Cael to log it as 'one more thing the instruments can't parse' and to note 'it is the third instrument to do it'. The draft follows must_include, and the word 'instrument' appears four times inside Cael's own log (ch01.md:45). Read as the more specific instruction governing the more general, which is the right resolution; but the Book-11 plant's language rule should be restated for Ch5, Ch14 and Ch22 so the recurrences do not inherit an ambiguity.

The REVISED block's clause 'Cael's ribs: quiet since the marsh; she reads the surface and finds them healed — the deep reading waits (Ch7)' is not paid as a surface reading. Oryn assesses him by eye and defers all contact: 'You're whole,' she said. 'I can see it from here.' (ch01.md:155). This is the safer choice against the packet's own prohibition on reading anyone without asking, and it keeps 'ask first, every time' clean in both directions — but the arc note asked for hands on ribs, and a human should confirm which the book wants before Ch7 is packeted.

obligations.must_include[3] frames Karis's ruler sentence as 'the winter's joke and once not as a joke'. The draft renders the doubling as rule and not-rule: 'She said it as she had said it at the Stair, as a rule, and then she looked at the cord in my hand for a while, and said it again, and it was not a rule the second time.' (ch01.md:43). The structural work — said twice, changed by nothing but her looking at the cord — is delivered and is arguably truer to Karis, who does not joke; recording the register change so the arc can accept or reject it.

The 129th (first snow) and the 130th (the ferry's last run) are never stated as numbers, though must_include[0] names both. Both are recoverable in one step from the opening date and 'The ferry went west yesterday' (ch01.md:3-5), and every entry is dated from the Line, so the day-count obligation is substantively met. Flagged only because a later continuity pass working from Book 8 alone has to do the subtraction.

'the third instrument this winter that reads everyone but me, if you count Oryn's hands as an instrument, and I do' (ch01.md:45). Oryn's hands read him in the autumn (B7 Ch13/14/22), not this winter; the qualifier makes the count of three work, but 'this winter' pulls the hands into a season they were not in. A four-word fix if the line-edit pass agrees.

Book 7 Ch24 has both edges touching 'the three centres without a hair of daylight and the fourth as near as the sheet allowed' (chapter-24.md:119), because the fourth circle is the carter's drawing, not a paced centre. The draft flattens this to 'it touched four' (ch01.md:41) and 'they do not stop touching all four' (ch01.md:35). Not a contradiction — the anomaly still reads — but the fourth circle's approximate status quietly hardens, and Ch19 enters that site on the strength of it.

'because' appears 38 times in 5,132 words. This is the cataloguing narrator's own subordination engine and it is doing real work in most instances, but the density is at the top of the series' range and Ch1 sets the book's baseline; worth measuring against B7's per-chapter figure in the line-edit pass rather than cutting by instinct.

Density is 5,132 words against 4,600 (+11.6%), inside the +/-15% band but using most of its upward room in the book's first chapter. Nothing to repair here; noted so the book-level average is watched from Ch2 rather than from Ch12.
strengths: The fixed closing text is byte-exact. A programmatic diff of the file's last line against the card returns an exact match, 'an index she can't read' included, and the file's last byte is that line. Do not let any repair pass touch line 211.

The chapter's hardest number is exactly right. Lira's 'Five months and twenty days.' (ch01.md:89) is 170 days after the bite on the 96th, which the draft itself re-states on the page ('where a hound's teeth had gone in on the ninety-sixth day', ch01.md:97), and which lands on the 266th given the departure on the 265th and the two-day road. It also silently fixes the series' month at thirty days and then holds that month across the ferryman's forecast and the mule's shed. This is the single most checkable thing in the chapter and it survives checking.

The release is staged as Lira's act, not the healer's, and the text says why: Oryn waits instead of reaching, 'because then it would have been the healer's and not the woman's' (ch01.md:101), and the sling comes off by a knot Lira learned to undo one-handed because she had had to. Five months of Book 7 restriction are paid in a gesture rather than a speech.

'Ask first, every time' is honored in both directions and dramatized as restraint on the protagonist's side. Oryn makes Lira ask ('Ask me.' / 'Will you mend it.'), and Cael declines a reading he could have taken: 'Cael did not count it. He wanted to and did not, because she had not asked him to' (ch01.md:123). The rule the tenth fragment came with is shown costing him something in the one chapter where nothing else costs anyone anything.

The Book-11 anomaly plant is exactly as deniable as it needs to be. Four people pace forty-two and he paces forty-one and a piece, three times, with the same cord and the same stones; the log files it in its own shorthand — 'Claim: something. Evidence: a cord, two edges, a hair. Ruling: hold.' (ch01.md:45) — attributes it to the unreadability he has carried since fourteen, and closes with 'Nobody at the table said that. Nobody said anything, and we went in to the fire, and the yard stayed forty-two strides for everyone else.' No theory, no gloss, and a protagonist confidently wrong in a way the reader cannot yet name.

Karis's ruler sentence is delivered twice and the second delivery is changed by nothing except where she is looking: 'and then she looked at the cord in my hand for a while, and said it again, and it was not a rule the second time' (ch01.md:43). The winter's turn is made without a single word of explanation.

Oryn's coming down is her route's arithmetic and not a favour, and the chapter refuses to soften it: 'I'd have been at Pike's plank in six days with or without a map. I'll be there in two. Get the mule.' followed by 'Nobody had asked her. He noted that — he noted everything — and put it in the place where he kept the things that were true about her' (ch01.md:169-171). The sixth chair is filled without anyone asking for it, which is the only way B7 said it could be.

The Tide cost is visible and specific: Oryn 'sitting back on her heels in the mud with her face the colour it went' (ch01.md:125), after a mending she refused in Book 7 for want of reserve and takes now because she has had a winter. The refusal and the acceptance are given the same reason, stated by her: 'I said that on a road with a man's shoulder to mend and a bank to sleep on. I've had a winter.' (ch01.md:115).

The chapter refuses to pre-pay Ch2 at the exact point it would be easiest. Karis's case is made in full, plainly, in her own order, and then: 'Nobody answered.' (ch01.md:191). Oryn's objection is left as a silence the narration explicitly declines to resolve — 'It was hers, and she would say it when she said it, and the ferry had not run' (ch01.md:193).
Ch5's seam is protected with one clause: 'There's a man there who is.' (ch01.md:189). Cleon is not named, so Cael's 'Who's Cleon?' four chapters on still lands as a first hearing.

The winter is rendered as an economy rather than a mood — eleven slips where there were forty, a meadow rate bought with a board-keeper's word, forty-one posts, two of Teague's a hand off true and reset without comment, a factor's own book, and Pike writing PAID under a season line he is deliberately leaving blank. Charter 3.7 in practice.
